name: variable used in a method but never declared vs both required variables actually declared
side_a: No_deduct when both the capacity variable and the current-amount variable appear as actual declarations in the class body (e.g. `private double capacity; private double amount;`), even if the names differ from the question's wording.
side_b: Deduct when one of the two required variables is only referenced inside a method and never declared anywhere in the class (the field simply does not exist), regardless of how the declared one is written.

name: explicit `private` on both instance variables vs default/package access declarations
side_a: No_deduct when each required instance variable declaration carries the explicit `private` keyword.
side_b: Deduct when the required instance variables are declared with no access modifier (default/package-private) or any non-private access, even if the types, names and constructor initialization are all otherwise correct.

name: updateAmount decreases the stored amount by the used quantity vs increases it (wrong sign / wrong arithmetic)
side_a: No deduct if the method reduces the tracked amount by the parameter (e.g. `amount = amount - used;`, `amount -= used;`, `this.currentAmount -= amountRemoved;`) before the refill check.
side_b: Deduct if the method moves the amount in the wrong direction — adding the used quantity instead of subtracting it (`amount = amount + used;`) — so the stored amount never reflects liquid removed.

name: Constructor sets the current-amount field to full capacity vs. leaves it uninitialized/undeclared
side_a: No deduction if the constructor explicitly stores the parameter into the current-amount field as well as the capacity field (e.g. `amount = cap;` / `this.currentAmount = capacity;`), so the bottle starts full and `updateAmount` has a valid starting value.
side_b: Deduct if the constructor only saves capacity and never initializes the current-amount field (or the field is never declared at all), so the subsequent subtraction operates on a default/undefined value.

name: Refill restores the amount to full capacity vs. to some other value (e.g. 25% of capacity)
side_a: No deduction if, when the level drops below 25% of capacity, the amount is reset to the full capacity value (`amount = capacity;`).
side_b: Deduct if the refill assigns anything other than full capacity, such as clamping the amount to `0.25 * capacity`.

name: Method has some return of a computed value vs. method body contains no return statement whatsoever (void-declared, result only stored)
side_a: Do not deduct when updateAmount actually ends with (or contains) a return statement that hands back the computed remaining amount, e.g. `return amount;` / `return this.currentAmount;`, regardless of how the value was derived or whether it also updated state.
side_b: Deduct when updateAmount contains no return statement at all — the method is declared `void` and merely assigns the result to a field/local (e.g. `public void updateAmount(double used) { amount -= used; ... }`). Nothing is returned, so the 'return the calculated amount' point is lost; this is separate from the header/return-type point in item 5, and is not excused by the fact that the correct value was computed and stored.
